reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails
clinicalPearls: Onychomadesis is complete, full-thickness separation of the nail plate beginning at the proximal end, which can progress to shedding of the whole nail
It represents the severe end of the same spectrum as Beau lines, both reflecting temporary arrest of nail matrix activity
When several nails are affected it usually follows a systemic insult such as a febrile illness, chemotherapy, or a major metabolic disturbance
It is a well-recognised sequel of hand, foot and mouth disease, appearing weeks after the acute infection has resolved
A single affected nail more often reflects local trauma to that matrix
The timing of the causative event can be estimated from the position of the separation and the rate of nail growth
It is generally self-limiting, and a new nail grows to replace the shed plate once matrix function recovers, so reassurance is central to management
reference.pathophysiology: Onychomadesis is caused by a complete but temporary halt in nail matrix activity, so that for a period no nail plate is produced and the newly forming proximal plate is disconnected from the older distal plate. When matrix function resumes, the new plate grows out and pushes off the detached older nail, which is shed. The insult may be systemic, such as a high fever, viral infection, cytotoxic drug, or metabolic upheaval that transiently diverts the matrix from plate production, or local trauma affecting a single digit; the more severe or prolonged the arrest, the more complete the separation compared with the partial groove of a Beau line.
additionalDifferentials: Beau lines (partial matrix arrest on the same spectrum)
Severe bullous disorders affecting the nail (for example epidermolysis bullosa or drug reactions)
Nail shedding in severe psoriasis or lichen planus
additionalInvestigations: History for recent febrile illness, viral infection (including hand, foot and mouth disease), or chemotherapy
Examination of all nails to determine single versus multiple involvement
Estimation of the timing of the insult from the level of separation
Screening for systemic or metabolic disease if no clear trigger is found
Review of recent medications, particularly cytotoxic agents
Mycology if fungal infection is a consideration
redFlags: Widespread nail shedding pointing to a significant systemic illness or drug reaction
Mucocutaneous blistering or a severe drug eruption requiring urgent evaluation
Signs of secondary infection of the exposed nail bed
Recurrent shedding suggesting cyclical systemic disease or ongoing exposure
reference.prognosis: Onychomadesis is usually self-limiting, and a new nail regrows over several months once the matrix recovers, with a good outcome provided the underlying trigger is transient and any secondary infection is prevented.
pitfalls: Alarming the patient rather than reassuring them when the cause is a self-limited illness
Failing to link post-viral nail shedding to a preceding hand, foot and mouth disease episode
Overlooking a serious systemic cause when many nails shed simultaneously
Neglecting protection of the exposed nail bed, allowing secondary infection
references: Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails and their Management
management: Reassure and manage expectantly, as the condition is self-limiting and a new plate regrows once matrix activity resumes
Identify and address the precipitating systemic trigger, such as a febrile illness, hand, foot and mouth disease, chemotherapy or a metabolic disturbance
Review causative medications, particularly cytotoxic agents, and modify where clinically possible
Protect the nail unit during regrowth and take measures to prevent secondary infection
Screen for underlying systemic or metabolic disease when no clear trigger is apparent
Monitor nail regrowth over several months to confirm recovery
